title: Getting Control of Your Life: The Five Stages of Mastering Workflow
coreMove: Run each incoming item through the five workflow stages before trusting your choice of what to do.
sourcePressure: The chapter lays out the workflow sequence: capture, clarify, organize, reflect, and engage, with actionable items sorted into do, delegate, or defer and non-actionable items into trash, incubate, or reference.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Memorizing five verbs as productivity vocabulary without showing the handoff from mixed stuff to defined options.
sourceAnchorNote: The source sidecar contains no chapter-specific named people, named studies, or named places. Use only the listed GTD terms, official metadata, or supported artifacts; do not invent anecdotes.

sourceAnchors.name: five stages of mastering workflow
sourceAnchors.detail: The sidecar names capture, clarify, organize, reflect, and engage as the chapter architecture.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The five stages are not a slogan; they are the path a messy input has to walk before it can become a clean choice.

sourceAnchors.name: two-minute rule
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar attaches the two-minute rule to immediate action during clarification.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The two-minute rule belongs at the decision point, not as a blanket excuse to chase every small task.

hook: stress is not about having too much to do
a messy desk proves the system is broken
counterintuition: the real problem is not time but attention
this is not about doing more but doing what matters
the simple move is actually the powerful one
tryThisNow: set a timer and write everything down
pick one task and make it specific
review your list and choose a priority
examples: timestamp plus name plus laptop plus decision repeated across all six examples
home kitchen clutter as mental-load shorthand

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.audience: a charge coordinator balancing clinical requests and room turnover
exampleSpecs.stakes: a family callback or cleaning hold could vanish between shifts

exampleSpecs.domain: a film festival volunteer desk sorting late filmmaker requests
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer lead with calls, badges, and screening changes arriving at once
exampleSpecs.stakes: a director may miss a screening because a change stayed in the wrong pile
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "Is this a ticket problem or a projection problem?" Thomas asks, forcing each request to become actionable, reference, or trash.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stack of lanyards beside a ringing desk phone

exampleSpecs.domain: a small architecture studio after a client sends fourteen markup comments
exampleSpecs.audience: a project coordinator who must turn comments into real work
exampleSpecs.stakes: a permit resubmission could slip if comments remain one mixed thread
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 4:10 p.m., Sophie decides not to answer the loudest comment first and instead sorts every markup into do, delegate, defer, or reference.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a marked-up facade drawing on a light table

exampleSpecs.domain: a fisheries field station after a storm damages monitoring gear
exampleSpecs.audience: a field scientist away from stable office tools
exampleSpecs.stakes: unprocessed damage notes could delay replacement sensors for a month
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Mikkel one missing sensor order to see that captured notes still failed when nobody clarified what they meant.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a salt-stained sensor case on a dock bench

exampleSpecs.domain: a nonprofit food pantry preparing for a Saturday distribution
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations lead with donations, volunteers, and client messages in motion
exampleSpecs.stakes: families could wait outside while tasks sit in a mixed notebook
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The folding tables are still upside down when Layla turns a page of mixed notes into calendar items, next actions, waiting-fors, and reference.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: folding tables stacked legs-up against a pantry wall

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional rail maintenance planner stuck with thirty minutes before a platform inspection
exampleSpecs.audience: a planner choosing work under changing constraints
exampleSpecs.stakes: a track closure decision could be made from urgency instead of a trusted menu
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You can feel the difference when Tomas chooses from context, time, energy, and priority instead of from the message that arrived last.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a clipboard clipped to a hi-vis vest
mustAvoid: making engage a vague priority lecture

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

skillTargets: apply the five stages in order
use two-minute rule only after clarification

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one fresh input and label its stage: captured only, clarified, organized, reviewed, or ready to engage.
